desc:
In one operation you may replace any single element of nums by any integer you like. Your goal is to make the array continuous: all elements distinct, and the difference between the largest and the smallest element equal to nums.length - 1 (so the final values are exactly x, x+1, ..., x+n-1 in some order, for some integer x).

Return the minimum number of operations needed.

For example, [1, 2, 3, 5, 6] gives 1 (replace 6 by 4), [4, 2, 5, 3] gives 0, and [1, 10, 100, 1000] gives 3.
hints: Decide which elements you will not touch. An untouched value is never useful twice, so repeats must be replaced anyway.

If the final array is the block x..x+n-1, you keep one element for each distinct original value inside that block. Maximise the number of distinct original values that fit into some block of n consecutive integers.
Sort the distinct values and slide a window: the window [i, j] is valid when v[j] - v[i] ≤ n - 1. The answer is n minus the largest valid window size.
editorial: Fix the final block of values x..x+n-1. Every original distinct value lying inside the block can stay (one copy of it), and every other element must be replaced, so the cost is n minus the number of distinct original values inside the block. Replacements can always fill the vacant slots, so nothing else is needed.

We want the block that contains the most distinct original values. It can be assumed to start at one of the distinct values, so sort the distinct values v and use two pointers: for each right end j, move i forward while v[j] - v[i] > n - 1. The best window size w gives the answer n - w. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the set.
